clue.text: Had flat here but moved, being unenthusiastic

indicators.note: the letters of the first three words are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone had a flat here but moved out, and is lukewarm about the whole business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moved' looks like the story of a house move, but it tells you to rearrange HAD FLAT HERE; 'being' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking enthusiasm means acting with only partial commitment, the sense of this compound adjective.

clue.text: The port knocks Edna out

indicators.note: with 'out' after the name, the woman's name is knocked out of shape
out of order, so the four letters of the name are rearranged

explanation.surface: A harbour town is so tough it knocks out a woman called Edna.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocks ... out' frames the name Edna and tells you to scramble it.
explanation.definitionFit: Aden is a seaport in Yemen on the Gulf of Aden.

clue.text: Be under the impression the charge is over a pound

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over, above, the second

parts.note: a charge or price is a fee
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling (from Latin libra)

explanation.surface: Someone suspects the price charged is more than a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is over' reads like 'exceeds', but in a down entry it places one piece above the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To believe something without proof is to sense it, an everyday synonym.

clue.text: Cover of new novel breaks a record

indicators.note: one piece breaks into the other, splitting it
made new, so the letters of the following word are rearranged

explanation.surface: The jacket of a fresh book shatters a sales record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges NOVEL to NVELO, which 'breaks' into EP; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrap something completely is to cover it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Artist about to put up a list

indicators.note: the artist's letters go about, around, the other piece

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist

indicators.note: in a down clue, put up means the word is written from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A painter is about to post a list on the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns TO into OT, and 'about' puts RA round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rota is a roster of people's duties in turn.

clue.text: Possibly saving firm in money difficulty

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the other
the word money is in difficulty, so it is shaken into a new order

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A company short of cash may be saved by careful management.
explanation.walkthrough: 'difficulty' rearranges MONEY to ENOMY, and 'in' puts CO inside it; 'Possibly' marks the definition as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrift is the act of cutting spending, so a cut made to save cash is an instance of it.

clue.text: Tom baker in a muddle going on board

indicators.note: the words Tom baker in a are in a muddle, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The actor Tom Baker is flustered as he boards a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a' looks like part of 'in a muddle', but those letters are part of the fodder with TOM BAKER; Tom Baker played Doctor Who.
explanation.definitionFit: Boarding a ship or aircraft is the act of setting out on a voyage.

clue.text: Get straight an argument over privileges

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over the second

parts.note: a set-to is a quarrel or fight

explanation.surface: A quarrel breaks out about who is entitled to what.
explanation.definitionFit: To put things in order is to make them straight, an idiom.

clue.text: Duck! It's captain hook's bosun!

explanation.surface: Someone shouts a warning to get down, naming the pirate's right-hand man.
explanation.definitionFit: Smee is a dialect name for a wild duck such as the wigeon, and Smee is the pirate boatswain in Peter Pan.

clue.text: Booking made with a certain misgiving

explanation.surface: A table was booked, but with some doubt about it.
explanation.definitionFit: A reservation is both an advance booking and a doubt or qualification held back.

clue.text: It isn't all go

explanation.surface: Life is not entirely full of activity.
explanation.definitionFit: A part is a portion, not the whole; to part is to leave or depart.

clue.text: A precaution against being fired

parts.note: reads like job security, but is a device on a gun that stops it discharging

explanation.surface: A worker takes steps to avoid getting the sack.
explanation.definitionFit: This mechanism locks a gun's trigger so it cannot shoot by accident.

clue.text: In close cooperation but offering nothing

parts.note: handing is passing or offering something
love is zero, nothing, in tennis scoring

explanation.surface: Partners work closely together yet contribute nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' is a link; LOVE means nil in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes two parties working in intimate partnership, like a glove fitting a hand.

clue.text: Forsake careless freedom

explanation.surface: Give up a carefree, uninhibited life.
explanation.definitionFit: To abandon is to desert; abandon as a noun is unrestrained freedom of manner.

clue.text: Proverbially hard on one's toes?

explanation.surface: Someone is famously tough when it comes to their feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Tough people are hard as nails, and toenails grow on the toes.

clue.text: Big kiss for a pound!

explanation.surface: A smacking great kiss is exchanged for a pound coin.
explanation.walkthrough: SMACKER is British slang for both a loud kiss and a pound sterling.
explanation.definitionFit: A smacker is a noisy kiss, and in British slang also a pound or dollar.

clue.text: Support the resistance

explanation.surface: Backing is given to the underground fighters.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand is a rest or holder, and to make a stand is to put up opposition.

clue.text: Function like one set of politicians

explanation.surface: Something works like a bunch of politicians.
explanation.definitionFit: A party is a social function and also a political grouping.

clue.text: The boy's in a whirl

explanation.surface: The lad is all of a spin.
explanation.definitionFit: Eddy is a boy's name, and an eddy is a swirling current of water or air.

clue.text: Game unsuitable for women

explanation.surface: A sport that women are barred from.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag is a deer hunted as game, and a stag party or event is for men only.

clue.text: Put out of sight

parts.note: reads as hiding something away, but also as taking away someone's power to see

explanation.surface: Something is hidden away.
explanation.definitionFit: To take away a person's vision is to make them sightless.

clue.text: Surprised expression of Irishman finding gold in capsized barge

indicators.note: one piece goes in the other
the barge has overturned, so its letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: An Irishman cries out on finding gold in an overturned boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capsized' rearranges BARGE to BEGRA, and 'in' puts OR inside; 'finding' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Begorra is a mild Irish exclamation, a euphemism for 'by God'.

clue.text: New income below five hundred is diabolical

indicators.note: in a down clue the second piece sits below the first

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for five hundred

indicators.note: made new, so the letters of income are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fresh income of under five hundred is a dreadful state of affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges INCOME to EMONIC, placed 'below' D; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish and fiendish describe both, a synonym.

clue.text: Statesmen making bets

explanation.surface: American politicians are placing wagers.
explanation.walkthrough: A Yankee is a British bookmakers' bet combining four selections; 'making' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Yankees are people from the United States, and a Yankee is a multiple bet on four horses.

clue.text: Full-back comes to sort out warm-up

indicators.note: the word is read back to front

parts.note: someone fed has eaten and is full

indicators.note: out of order, so the letters of sort are rearranged

explanation.surface: A football defender arrives to organise the pre-match routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Full-back' reads as the football position, but it splits: FED turned 'back' gives DEF; 'out' rearranges SORT to ROST; 'comes to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Thawing frozen food means bringing its temperature up, a synonym.

clue.text: Turning point in a revolution

parts.note: sounds like a decisive moment in an uprising, but describes the rod a wheel spins on

explanation.surface: The decisive moment in a political uprising.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheel rotates on this shaft, the pivot of each turn.

clue.text: Being old, agreed about being dropped

indicators.note: the letters for about are dropped from the word agreed

parts.note: RE is Latin for about, concerning

explanation.surface: Elderly, and agreed on regarding the matter of being let go.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderly people have lived many years, the adjective's plain sense.

clue.text: Strike action when mates turn up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning the word up writes it from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Industrial action begins when one's workmates arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike action' reads as a walkout but means a blow; 'when' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A smack with the open hand is a blow, so it is the action of hitting.

clue.text: Heap of carpets

explanation.surface: A stack of rugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A pile is a stack, and the pile of a carpet is its raised surface of fibres.

clue.text: First offence?

parts.note: reads as a minor legal matter, but refers to the very first wrong, by Adam and Eve

explanation.surface: Someone is in court for the first time.
explanation.definitionFit: Christian doctrine holds that all inherit the sin of Adam, the earliest wrongdoing.

clue.text: Chap found walking along the coast

explanation.surface: A man is spotted strolling beside the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: COVE is old British slang for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Cove is dated slang for a fellow, and a cove is a small bay one meets on a coastal walk.

clue.text: Wasn't up to scratch, suffering from some disability

explanation.surface: Someone fell short because of an impairment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratch' in golf is a zero handicap, so a golfer who is not scratch plays off a handicap.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer given strokes is not playing at scratch level, and the word also describes physical impairment.
